c1-69.title: Checking a conflict report
c1-69.story: Anna spent Saturday fact-checking a draft report for her journalism professor in Kyiv. The writer had called one fighter's pistol a [[magnum]], but the photo clearly showed a small-[[caliber]] handgun. A paragraph about a bridge fire claimed [[sabotage]], and the police had in fact recovered a [[detonator]] near the rails. Max, reading over her shoulder, asked why the report used so many different labels for armed groups. Anna explained that an [[insurgent]] fights against a government, while a [[separatist]] wants a region to break away. She added that calling someone a [[jihadist]] is a serious claim, and that the word [[jihad]] itself originally means "struggle." The trickiest sentence named one state as the [[aggressor]], so she checked it against three independent sources before leaving it in. By evening, her notes were longer than the report, and the professor thanked her for catching every slip.

c1-70.title: Genes and mutants
c1-70.story: Taras came home excited about a movie in which a [[mutant]] could change the color of his skin at will. Anna, who had a genetics exam on Monday, decided to turn his question into a study break. She explained that skin color depends mostly on a [[pigment]] called melanin, and that cells need a special [[enzyme]] to produce it. "So is the secret hidden somewhere in his [[genome]]?" Taras asked. Partly, she said, but a cell also needs the right [[receptor]] to catch the signal that switches production on. Max's sister Sofia, who was doing an internship at a [[biotech]] startup, joined the video call and confirmed that real science moves much more slowly than the movies. Taras looked disappointed for a moment, then announced that he would become a scientist and speed things up.

c1-71.title: Inside the atom
c1-71.story: Anna's grandfather, a retired engineer, took her and Taras to the science museum on a rainy Sunday. In the first hall, a glowing model showed a single [[proton]] at the center of a [[hydrogen]] atom. Taras pressed a button, and the model added a [[neutron]], turning the atom into a heavier [[isotope]] called deuterium. "And what's inside those little balls?" he asked, so Grandpa pointed to a screen where each [[quark]] appeared as a tiny colored dot. Next came a glass ball full of [[plasma]], where purple threads followed Taras's fingers across the surface. Grandpa explained that electricity had pulled electrons away, turning the gas atoms inside into [[ions|ion]]. In the last room, a model of a nuclear [[reactor]] showed how much of the country's power is produced. Before leaving, Taras caught a single [[photon]] on a light detector, and the counter clicked once. On the way home, he declared that atoms were cooler than dinosaurs, and Grandpa smiled as if he had finally won a long argument.

c1-72.title: In the electricity lab
c1-72.story: In Thursday's lab session, Anna and Max had to build a simple circuit and measure everything carefully. First, Max checked the [[voltage]] of their battery, which read just under nine [[volts|volt]]. Anna added a resistor of two hundred [[ohms|ohm]] and reminded him that the professor wanted every value written in [[SI]] units. For the next step, they drew a thick line with a soft pencil, because [[graphite]] conducts electricity surprisingly well. A small green [[indicator]] lit up the moment the current passed through the drawing. Their table also held samples of [[nickel]], [[cobalt]], and [[chrome]], and they had to find out which ones a magnet would pick up. Finally, the professor struck a tuning fork next to a second one, and [[resonance]] made the second fork hum on its own. Max was so pleased that he hummed along, and Anna described it in the report as an unplanned experiment.

c1-73.title: In the chemistry lab
c1-73.story: On her first day as a lab assistant, Anna got a tour of the chemistry stockroom from her friend Ira, who had worked there for a year. Ira began with safety: everyone wears [[latex]] gloves, and people who are allergic will find nitrile ones in the second drawer. The locked cabinet held [[cyanide]], which no student was allowed to touch without a supervisor. On the open shelves stood jars of iron [[oxide]], a bag of sodium [[chloride]], and fertilizer samples rich in [[nitrate]] and [[phosphate]]. Near the window, a bottle of [[ethanol]] was kept for cleaning equipment, next to an old brown bottle of [[ether]] from the 1970s. Ira then opened a drawer of plastic samples and explained that each one was a different [[polymer]]. The last item was a set of [[silicone]] molds, which, Ira admitted, were not for science at all but for the lab's monthly cake day. Anna laughed and decided that this was going to be a very good job.

c1-74.title: A poster about space
c1-74.story: Anna and Max spent the evening designing a poster for the university's astronomy night. Max painted the background as a dark [[gradient]], from deep blue at the bottom to black at the top. In the center, Anna placed a chart of the night sky divided into four parts and put the brightest star in the upper left [[quadrant]]. Next to it, she drew a [[vector]] to show the direction and speed of a passing comet. Max insisted on adding the comet's orbit equation, even though few visitors would check whether the [[coefficient]] in front of x was right. Their main text described the [[genesis]] of the [[cosmos]], based on a simulation the physics department had run on a computer [[cluster]] for weeks. A small box explained why the sun reaches its [[zenith]] much higher over Kyiv in June than in December. When Max complained that constellations were just a human [[construct]], Anna pointed out a clear [[parallel]] with borders on a map: invented, but still useful. The poster won second place, and the prize was a pizza, which Max called the true center of the universe.

c1-75.title: Kings, dukes, and nobles
c1-75.story: Lisa came over to study for their European history exam, and Anna's little brother Taras insisted on helping. He took the flashcards and began with the easiest question: who ranks higher, a [[duke]] or a [[baron]]? Lisa answered correctly, then added that in England an [[earl]] sits between the two. The next card asked what a [[regent]] does, and Anna explained that one rules while the [[monarch]] is still a child. Taras liked the word [[kaiser]] so much that he started using it as a nickname for the family cat. Lisa explained that the [[gentry]] owned land but usually had no titles, unlike a true [[aristocrat]]. The last card said only "[[sovereign]]," and Anna said it was a formal word for a king or queen who holds supreme power. By midnight, the cat was wearing a paper crown, and the girls felt ready for anything the exam might bring.

c1-76.title: Empires of the East
c1-76.story: Anna took her grandmother to a new exhibition about the empires of the East at the history museum. The first room showed a map of a vast [[caliphate]] that once stretched from Spain to Central Asia. Next came a model of a [[sultan]]'s palace, including the private quarters known as the [[harem]], where his wives and children lived. Grandma admitted that she had always pictured the [[steppe]] as endless grass, and the huge photos proved her right. In a corner, a stuffed [[yak]] reminded visitors how people crossed cold mountain passes with heavy loads. The final hall was dedicated to a stone [[citadel]] on a hill that had served as the last [[bastion]] against invaders for two centuries. On the way out, Grandma bought a postcard of a shaggy mountain animal for Taras, who would certainly want to ride one.
